readings.c1s2:
¶
'''wind-contusion''' (wind′kọn-tū″zhọn), ''n.'' In ''surg.'', a contusion, such as rupture of the liver or concussion of the brain, unaccompanied by any external mark of violence, supposed to be produced by the air when rapidly displaced by the velocity of a projectile, as a cannon-ball. {{smaller|It is now, however, considered to be occasioned by the projectile itself striking the body in an oblique direction, the comparative escape of the external soft tissues being accounted for by the degree of obliquity with which the missile impinges on the elastic skin, together with the position of the internal structures injured relatively to the impingement of the ball on one side and hard resisting substances on another. Also called ''windage''.}}

'''wind-cutter''' (wind′kut″ėr), ''n.'' In ''organ-building'', the upper lip of the mouth of a flue-pipe, against which the stream of air impinges when the pipe is sounded.

'''wind-dial''' (wind′dī″ạl), ''n.'' A dial showing the changes in the direction of the wind by means of an index or pointer connected with a wind-vane.
{{smaller block|The ''Wind Dial'' lately set up at Grigsby’s Coffee and Chocolate House, behind the Royal Exchange, being the first and only one in any publick House in England, and having given great Satisfaction to all that have seen it, and being of Constant use to those that are in any wise Concerned in Navigation.
{{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, [II. 56.}}}}

'''wind-dog''' (wind′dog), ''n.'' A name popularly applied to fragments of rainbows seen on detached clouds. Also ''wind-gall''.

'''wind-dropsy''' (wind′drop″si), ''n.'' Emphysema; tympanites.

'''wind-egg''' (wind′eg), ''n.'' An infecund or otherwise imperfect egg, as one which will produce
readings.c1s3:
nothing but wind (gas); a soft-shelled egg, such as may be laid by a hen that is comparatively old or has been injured.

'''winder'''<sup>1</sup> (wīn′dėr), ''n.'' [< ''wind''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who winds, rolls, or coils: as, a bobbin-''winder''.
{{smaller block|They consist of sewing boys, shoe-binders, ''winders'' for weavers, and girls for all kinds of slop needlework.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 353.}}}}
'''2.''' An instrument or a machine for winding thread, etc. {{smaller|(''a'') A contrivance like a small windlass revolving a spool or reel upon which the thread is wound. (''b'') A large adjustable frame which can be passed through the opening of a skein and then increased in diameter so as to hold it firmly for winding off. (''c'') A small stick, strip, or notched slate upon which thread can be wound: a substitute for a spool or reel.}} '''3.''' The key or utensil used to wind up the spring-work of a roasting-jack.
{{smaller block|To keep troublesome servants out of the kitchen, always leave the ''winder'' sticking on the jack to fall on their heads.
{{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (Cook).}}}}
'''4.''' A plant that twists itself round others.
{{smaller block|''Winders'' and creepers; as ivy, briony, hops.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 536.}}}}
'''5.''' A winding-step of a staircase.

'''winder'''<sup>2</sup> (wīn′dėr), ''n.'' [< ''wind''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who winds or sounds a horn.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Winder'' of the horn,
When snouted wild-boars routing tender corn
Anger our huntsman.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
'''2''' (win′dėr). A blow which takes away the breath.—'''3.''' A fan. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''winder<sup>2</sup>''' (win′dėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''winder''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''; prob. in part a dial. corruption of *''winner'' for ''winnow''.] To fan; clean or winnow with a fan: as, to ''winder'' grain. ''Brockett.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''windfall''' (wind′fâl), ''n.'' [< ''wind''<sup>1</sup> + ''fall''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Something blown down by the wind, as fruit from a tree, or a number of trees in a forest.
{{smaller block|When they did spread, and their boughs were become too great for their stem, they became a ''windfall'' upon the sudden.
{{right|''Bacon'', True Greatness of Kingdoms and Estates (ed. 1887).}}
She ’s nobbut gone int’ t’ orchard, to see if she can find ''wind-falls'' enough for t’ make a pie or two for t’ lads.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, vi.}}}}
'''2.''' An unexpected piece of good fortune, as an unexpected legacy.
{{smaller block|This man, who otherwise beforetime was but poor and needy, by these ''windfalls'' and unexpected cheats became very wealthy. ''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch’s Morals, p. 1237.}}
'''3.''' The tract of fallen trees, etc., which shows the path of a tornado.—'''4.''' A violent gust of wind rushing from coast-ranges and mountains to the sea.—'''5.''' The down-rush of air occurring on the leeward side of a hill or mountain at a distance from its base.

'''windfall†''' (wind′fâl), ''a.'' Windfallen. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>You shall have leaves and ''windfall'' boughs enow,
Near to these woods, to roast your meat withal.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe and Nashe'', Dido, Queen of Carthage, i. 1. 172.}}}}

'''windfallen''' (wind′fâ″ln), ''a.'' Blown down by the wind.
{{smaller block|To gather ''windfall’n'' sticks.
{{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xiii. 182.}}}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''windfanner''' (wind′fan″ėr), ''n.'' Same as ''windhover.''

'''wind-fertilized''' (wind′fėr″ti-līzd), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', fertilized with pollen borne by the wind, as flowers; anemophilous, as conifers, grasses, sedges, etc.

'''windfish''' (wind′fish), ''n.'' The fall-fish, or silver chub, ''Semotilus bullaris'', the largest cyprinoid of eastern North America. See ''Semotilus.''

'''wind-flower''' (wind′flou″ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' A plant of the genus ''Anemone'', chiefly the wood-anemone, ''A. nemorosa:'' so called by translation of the classic name of an anemone or other plant anciently associated with the wind. {{smaller|The wind-loving reputation of this plant appears to have been conferred chiefly by the name. The wind-flower is a small herb, found in Europe, northwestern Asia, and North America, bearing a whorl of three trifoliate leaves and a single delicate white or outwardly pinkish vernal flower. The American pasque-flower, ''A. patens'', var. ''Nuttalliana'', bears the name specifically in the western United States.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Bide thou where the poppy blows,
With ''wind-flowers'' frail and fair.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Arctic Lover.}}}}
'''2.''' The marsh-gentian, ''Gentiana Pneumonanthe. Treas. of Bot.''

'''wind-furnace''' (wind′fėr″nạ̄s), ''n.'' Any form of furnace using the natural draft of a chimney without the aid of a bellows or blower; a natural-draft furnace; a laboratory-furnace provided with a tall chimney.
{{smaller block|The crucible is then placed in a ''wind-furnace'', and slowly heated as long as fumes escape. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 553.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''wind-hatch''' (wind′hach), ''n.'' In ''mining'', the opening or place where ore is taken out of the earth.

'''windhawk''' (wind′hâk), ''n.'' The windhover or kestrel.

'''wind-herb''' (wind′ėrb), ''n.'' See ''Phlomis''.

'''wind-house''' (wind′hous), ''n.'' A house built partly underground to serve as a shelter or place of refuge in hurricanes.

'''windhover''' (wind′huv″ėr), ''n.'' A kind of hawk, the kestrel, ''Falco tinnunculus'' or ''Tinnunculus alaudarius'': so called from its hovering in the face of the wind. See ''kestrel''. Also called ''windbibber'', ''windcuffer'', ''windfanner'', ''windhawk'', ''windsucker'', ''vanner-hawk'', ''staniel'', etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>About as long
As the ''wind-hover'' hangs in balance.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}

'''windily''' (win′di-li), ''adv.'' With high wind; in a way that betokens wind.
{{smaller block|The stars were glittering ''windily'' even before this crimson melted out of the east.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Sailor’s Sweetheart, iv.}}}}

'''windiness''' (win′di-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state of being windy or tempestuous: as, the ''windiness'' of the weather or season.—'''2.''' Flatulence.—'''3.''' Tendency to generate wind (gas): as, the ''windiness'' of vegetables.—'''4.''' Tumor; puffiness; vanity; boastfulness.
{{smaller block|The swelling ''windiness'' of much knowledge.
{{right|''Brerewood’s Languages'', Pref.}}}}

'''winding'''<sup>1</sup> (wīn′ding), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''wind''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Curving; spiral: as, a ''winding'' stair.

{{smaller block|’Twould ''wind-break'' a mule to vie burdens with her.
{{right|''Ford.''}}}}

'''windbroach†''' (wind′brōch), ''n.'' The hurdy-gurdy or vielle.
{{smaller block|Nero, a base blind fiddler, or player on that instrument which is called a ''windbroach.''
{{right|''Urquhart,'' tr. of Rabelais, ii. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|For an old man to pretend to talk wisely is like a musician’s endeavouring to fumble out a fine sonata upon a ''wind-broach.''
{{right|''Tom Brown,'' Works, II. 234. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wind-broken''' (wind′brō″kn), ''p. a.'' Diseased in the respiratory organs; having the power of breathing impaired by chest-disease: as, a ''wind-broken'' horse. Also ''broken-winded.''

'''wind-changing''' (wind′chān″jing), ''a.'' Changeful as the wind; fickle. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Wind-changing'' Warwick now can change no more.
{{right|''Shak.,'' 3 Hen. VI., v. 1. 57.}}}}

'''wind-chart''' (wind′chärt), ''n.'' A chart showing the wind-directions at a given time, or the directions prevailing during any period of the year over any region of the earth. {{smaller|Wind-charts for the ocean, of which the “Wind and Current Charts” of the British Admiralty and the “Pilot Charts” of the United States Hydrographic Office are examples, constitute an important aid to navigators.}}

'''wind-chest''' (wind′chest), ''n.'' In ''organ-building,'' a chest or box immediately below the pipes or reeds, from which the compressed air is admitted to them by means of valves or pallets. See ''organ''<sup>1</sup> and ''reed-organ.''

'''wind-colic''' (wind′kol″ik), ''n.'' Intestinal pain caused by flatulence.

{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, vi.}}}}

{{smaller block|This man, who otherwise beforetime was but poor and needy, by these ''windfalls'' and unexpected cheats became very wealthy.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch’s Morals, p. 1237.}}}}
'''3.''' The tract of fallen trees, etc., which shows the path of a tornado.—'''4.''' A violent gust of wind rushing from coast-ranges and mountains to the sea.—'''5.''' The down-rush of air occurring on the leeward side of a hill or mountain at a distance from its base.

A plant of the genus ''Anemone'', chiefly the wood-anemone, ''A. nemorosa:'' so called by translation of the classic name of an anemone or other plant anciently associated with the wind. {{smaller|The wind-loving reputation of this plant appears to have been conferred chiefly by the name. The American pasque-flower, ''A. patens'', var. ''Nuttalliana'', bears the name specifically in the western United States.}}

With ''wind-flowers'' frail and fair.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Arctic Lover.}}}}
'''2.''' The marsh-gentian, ''Gentiana Pneumonanthe. Treas. of Bot.''

{{smaller block|The crucible is then placed in a ''wind-furnace'', and slowly heated as long as fumes escape. {{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 553.}}}}

'''wind-gage''' (wind′gāj), ''n.'' '''1.''' An instrument for ascertaining the velocity and force of wind; an anemometer. See ''anemometer.''—'''2.''' An apparatus or contrivance for measuring or indicating the amount of the pressure of the wind in the wind-chest of an organ.—'''3.''' ''Milit.'', a graduated attachment to the sights of a firearm or cannon by which allowance can be made, in aiming, for the effect of the wind upon the projectile.

'''wind-gall<sup>1</sup>''' (wind′gâl), ''n.''   [< ''wind<sup>2</sup>'' + ''gall<sup>2</sup>''.]   Distension of the synovial bursa at the fetlock-joint of the horse, such as may be felt on each side of the tendons behind the joint. Also called ''puff.''
{{smaller block|His horse, . . . full of ''windgalls'', sped with spavins.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2. 53.}}}}
{{smaller block|Neither Spavin, Splinter, nor ''Wind-gall.''
{{right|''Etherege'', She Would if She Could, ii. 2.}}}}

'''wind-gall<sup>2</sup>''' (wind′gâl), ''n.''   [< ''wind<sup>2</sup>'' + ''gall<sup>2</sup>''; as in ''water-gall, weather-gall.'']   Same as ''wind-dog.''
{{smaller block|“Wind-dogs,” . . . fragments or pieces (as it were) of rainbows (sometimes called ''wind-galls'') seen on detached clouds. {{right|''Fitz Roy'', Weather Book, p. 23.}}}}

'''wind-galled''' (wind′gâld), ''a.'' Having wind-galls.
{{smaller block|Did you think I was ''Wind-gall’d?'' I can sing too, if I please. {{right|''Steele'', Tender Husband, iii. 1.}}}}

'''wind-gap''' (wind′gap), ''n.'' See ''gap'', 2.

'''wind-gun''' (wind′gun), ''n.'' Same as ''air-gun.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Forc’d from ''wind-guns'', lead itself can fly,
And pond’rous slugs cut swiftly through the sky.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, i. 181.}}}}

'''wind-hatch''' (wind′hach), ''n.'' In ''mining'', the opening or place where ore is taken out of the earth.

'''windhawk''' (wind′hâk), ''n.'' The windhover or kestrel.

'''wind-herb''' (wind′ėrb), ''n.'' See ''Phlomis''.

'''wind-house''' (wind′hous), ''n.'' A house built partly underground to serve as a shelter or place of refuge in hurricanes.

'''windhover''' (wind′huv″ėr), ''n.'' A kind of hawk, the kestrel, ''Falco tinnunculus'' or ''Tinnunculus alaudarius'': so called from its hovering in the face of the wind. See ''kestrel''. Also called ''windbibber'', ''windcuffer'', ''windfanner'', ''windhawk'', ''windsucker'', ''vanner-hawk'', ''staniel'', etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>About as long
As the ''wind-hover'' hangs in balance.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}}

'''windily''' (win′di-li), ''adv.'' With high wind; in a way that betokens wind.
{{smaller block|The stars were glittering ''windily'' even before this crimson melted out of the east.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Sailor’s Sweetheart, iv.}}}}

'''windiness''' (win′di-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state of being windy or tempestuous: as, the ''windiness'' of the weather or season.—'''2.''' Flatulence.—'''3.''' Tendency to generate wind (gas): as, the ''windiness'' of vegetables.—'''4.''' Tumor; puffiness; vanity; boastfulness.
{{smaller block|The swelling ''windiness'' of much knowledge.
{{right|''Brerewood’s Languages'', Pref.}}}}

'''winding'''<sup>1</sup> (wīn′ding), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''wind''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Curving; spiral: as, a ''winding'' stair. {{smaller block|The staires are ''winding'', having a stately roofe.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 35.}}}}
'''2.''' Full of bends or turns: as, a ''winding'' path.
{{smaller block|The ascent [of mount Tabor] is so easy that we rode up the north side by a ''winding'' road.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 64.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Across the court-yard, into the dark
Of the ''winding'' pathway in the park,
Curate and lantern disappear.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Baron of St. Castine.}}}}
'''3.''' Warped; twisted; bent; crooked: as, a ''winding'' surface.

'''winding'''<sup>1</sup> (wīn′ding), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wyndynge''; verbal n. of ''wind''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A turn or turning; a bend; flexure; meander: as, the ''windings'' of a road or stream.
{{smaller block|The degise, endentyng, barrynge, owndynge, palynge, ''wyndynge'' or bendynge, and semblable wast of clooth in vanitee.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [the ways] were wonderfull hard, all stony and full of ''windings''.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|To follow the ''windings'' of this river.
{{right|''Addison'', Remarks on Italy (Works, ed. Bohn, I. 537).}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''windings'' of the marge.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Edwin Morris.}}}}
'''2.''' A twist in any surface, so that all its parts do not lie in the same plane; a casting or warping. ''Gwilt.''—'''Compound winding.''' {{smaller|When the field-magnets of a dynamo are fitted with two coils, one of which is placed in circuit with the armature and external leads, while the other is connected across the terminals as a shunt, the dynamo is said to be ''compound wound'', and the winding ''compound winding.''—'''Differential winding.''' See ''differential.''—'''In winding''', warped; out of the straight: applied by joiners to a piece of wood when two of its opposite corners stand higher than the other two.—'''Out of winding''', brought to a plane: said of a surface: a workmen’s phrase.—'''Series winding.''' A dynamo is said to be ''series wound'', or to have a ''series winding'', when its field-magnet coil is joined in series with the armature coil.—'''Shunt winding.''' When the field-magnet coils of a dynamo are designed for, and connected as, a shunt on the armature coil, the dynamo is said to be ''shunt wound'', and the method of winding ''shunt winding.''}}

'''winding<sup>2</sup>''' (wīn′ding), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''wind<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.'']   A call by the boatswain’s whistle.

'''winding-engine''' (wīn′ding-en″jin), ''n.'' Any steam-motor employed to turn a drum around which a hoisting-rope is drawn; in a mine, an engine by which the ropes are wound on and unwound from the drums, for raising or lowering the bucket, kibble, or cage on which the mined material is brought to the surface. Also called ''drawing-engine'' and ''hoisting-engine.''

'''windingly''' (wīn′ding-li), ''adv.'' In a winding manner; with curves, bends, or turns.
{{smaller block|<poem>The stream that creeps
''Windingly'' by it.</poem>{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}

'''winding-pendant''' (wīn′ding-pen″dạnt), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a pendant hooked at the fore- or main-masthead with its bight secured as far out as necessary on the foreyard or main-yard, and having a heavy tackle, called a ''winding-tackle'', depending from its lower end, used for lifting heavy weights.

'''winding-rope''' (wīn′ding-rōp), ''n.'' In ''mining'', the rope which connects the cage with the drum of the winding-engine. {{smaller|Formerly the winding-ropes}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
